newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - US players seek refuge from EMU storm.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US players seek refuge from EMU storm.

text.p: Dangerous crosscurrents swirling through Europe's financial bourses as its leaders gird for monetary union have U.S. investors looking for more predictable bets in dollar-bloc countries.

European convergence trades offer lucrative, if risky, short-term plays on the mark crosses, but their volatility and Europe's relative economic weakness have many buyers looking at U.S., Canadian, Australian and British assets.
"The market prefers to own the Anglo-Saxon market currencies," said Michael Rosenberg at Merrill Lynch.

"There is clearly a preference to own currencies where growth prospects are strong and to move away from currencies where growth prospects look relatively bleak," said Rosenberg, who heads international fixed-income research at Merrill.
Continental Europe remains mired in a deep economic slump, even as the dollar bloc nations enjoy steady, low inflation growth, experts noted.
That enhances the appeal of the currencies and some of the bond markets outside of Europe, analysts said.

In Australia, bond yields have backed up in recent sessions and the Aussie dollar has climbed 3.5 cents versus the U.S. dollar over the last three weeks. That makes the markets down under look mighty tempting, analysts said.
"We like Australia. The yield spreads are attractive; the currency is undervalued; industrial metal prices are strong. It really has a lot going for it," said Rosenberg.

Aussie 10-year paper currently yields about 7.90 percent, 130 basis points more than comparable U.S. debt. If the nation produces a conservative, noninflationary budget this year, that spread could narrow to below 100, said John Krey, chief investment strategist at Barclays Global Asset Management.
"Spreads have widened out, but there's room for the spread to narrow into the 90s or 80s with a good budget, so we're holding our Aussie positions," Krey said.

But U.S. investors have not fully abandoned European markets. While the mark has staggered steadily lower against the dollar, it still offers occasional windfalls versus peripheral European units when EMU enthusiasm wanes.
Comments over the last week from German and Italian officials raised doubts that EMU would start on time and sent the mark sharply higher against the lira and Spanish peseta.
But dollar/mark reached a 34-month high, dimming the appeal of bunds. Still, German yields remain competitive with other European paper, Krey noted.
"If everything falls through on EMU, Switzerland, the U.S. and Canada will benefit the most, but it can't be all that bad for Germany," he added.
Krey cited sterling and the Norwegian crown, two currencies not slated to join the EMU party, as safe places to park money as the January 1999 launch date nears.

"There is going to be a runup in early 1998 when the core (EMU) currencies are going to be announced. It's safe to say there's going to be turmoil there and a position in sterling or Norway would be very much in order," he said.

Safe havens may also be found in such unlikely locations as Greece and Portugal, two countries seen having little chance of participating in the EMU launch, according to international strategist Richard Koss at MFR Inc.
"Nobody expects these people to make the first round of EMU, so there won't be the same kind of disappointment if this thing goes into a tailspin," Koss said.
